spec: Implement the Pod City automation bridge as a Python directory watcher rather than a Git-hook workflow. Treat this task as superseding any earlier queued watcher task. Build the bridge as a safe, local, filesystem-backed handoff between Manus as Lead Architect and Claude Code as Implementation Agent. First, finalize the task.json contract so each task pod must include task_id, priority, spec_file, spec, acceptance_criteria, and files. The task_id must be a unique string; priority must be high, med, or low; spec_file must point to the canonical shared workspace specification file; spec must be the task-specific authoritative work instruction; acceptance_criteria must be an explicit list of testable completion conditions; and files must list expected touched files or directories. Second, establish ARCHITECTURE_SPECS.md as the canonical shared spec file that both the architecture agent and the implementation agent must read before changing code. Manus must write or update architecture intent there, Claude Code must read it before execution, and both agents must treat it as the durable shared source of truth alongside the current active pod. Third, update CLAUDE.md so Claude Code is standardized as the Pod City Implementation Agent. CLAUDE.md must explicitly state that Claude Code monitors ./pods/inbox/, reads the active task JSON, reads the shared spec_file before modifying files, validates the task requirements against the existing codebase, implements only the requested scope, and moves completed task pods through the lifecycle. CLAUDE.md must also define CI Review Standards for Greptile or Greploop review context, including repository-specific coding standards such as secure defaults, parameterized queries for database access, least-privilege configuration, no hardcoded secrets, explicit tests for changed behavior, and no unrelated application changes. Fourth, create a Python watcher script, preferably .claude/scripts/bridge.py or .claude/scripts/watch_pod_inbox.py, that monitors ./pods/inbox/ for task JSON files using watchdog when available, with a simple polling fallback if watchdog is not installed. The script must detect task.json and any other *.json task file, wait until the file is stable before reading it, validate the required fields, move the task into ./pods/active/ while processing, and invoke Claude Code in non-interactive headless mode with a configurable command. Fifth, use claude -p as the preferred headless execution mechanism when the claude command is available. The default command template should be equivalent to claude -p "Read ARCHITECTURE_SPECS.md and implement the task defined in <task-file>. Return machine-readable JSON describing success, changed files, tests, review requirements, infrastructure requirements, git handoff status, and notes." --allowedTools "Bash,Read,Edit" --max-turns 10 --output-format json. Where available, also support an alternate claude-code --execute --input <task-file> style command through configuration. The bridge must not use interactive watch mode as its default execution path. Sixth, support structured execution output. If the installed Claude Code command supports JSON output, --output-format json, or --json-schema, configure the bridge to request a structured result containing success status, changed files, test results, review requirements, infrastructure requirements, git handoff status, and notes. If structured output is unavailable, the bridge must capture stdout and stderr and parse only conservative lifecycle signals; do not infer success from vague text alone. Seventh, enforce safe automation constraints. The bridge must support configurable allowed tools and max turns so headless runs do not stall or enter endless loops. The bridge must verify and clearly report whether required execution environment variables such as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY are available before attempting headless execution, while never logging or committing secret values. The bridge must not enable --dangerously-skip-permissions by default. If a local operator explicitly chooses to use --dangerously-skip-permissions for fully autonomous local execution, that setting must be disabled by default, placed only in a git-ignored local config such as .claude/pod-bridge.local.json, documented as risky, and never committed. Eighth, implement lifecycle movement. If Claude Code succeeds, the quality gate passes, and the Git handoff either succeeds or is explicitly disabled in local dry-run mode, move the processed task file from ./pods/active/ to ./pods/archive/. If Claude Code fails, schema validation fails, Greptile fails, Git handoff fails when required, or quality confidence is below threshold, annotate the task JSON with result metadata and move it to ./pods/failed/. Ninth, integrate the Greptile quality gate as a post-execution review step, isolated from the code-generation step. The same Claude session that generated code must not be treated as the reviewer. The bridge should run greptile review --path . when a Greptile CLI is available, and it should document how to enable the Greptile plugin in Claude Code through the /plugins flow and how to use /greploop or /check-pr manually when the CLI is unavailable. Use confidence >= 5 as the pass threshold. If Greptile is unavailable, the script must not silently pass; it should either fail closed by default or expose an explicit configuration flag documenting local development bypass behavior. Tenth, create and preserve the lifecycle directories ./pods/inbox/, ./pods/active/, ./pods/archive/, and ./pods/failed/ using .gitkeep placeholders as needed. Eleventh, add a Git handoff stage that runs only after successful Claude execution and passing Greptile review. The handoff must verify git status, stage only task-approved paths or an explicitly configured allowlist, create a clear automation commit, and push to the configured remote branch so the repository's deployment automation can trigger the KVM environment. The bridge must support dry-run mode that prints the exact git add, commit, and push commands without running them. A real git push must be controlled by local configuration and must never commit secrets, logs, .claude/pod-bridge.local.json, or unrelated changes. Twelfth, add a deployment-trigger verification stage immediately after any real git push. The bridge must record the pushed branch and commit SHA, then verify that the repository automation intended to deploy to the KVM environment has been triggered. Verification may use configured GitHub Actions checks, deployment statuses, repository webhooks, a configured CI status command, or another local verification command, but it must be explicit and logged. If no deployment automation is discoverable in the repository or local configuration, the bridge must report that the KVM trigger cannot be verified and must not claim production deployment success. Thirteenth, add an infrastructure handoff stage that is triggered by the Git repository's deployment automation after the push, rather than by Manus directly. The bridge may record infrastructure requirements and deployment metadata for KVM8, Terraform, or Ansible, but direct provisioning commands remain disabled by default unless explicitly enabled in local ignored configuration. By default, the bridge logs that deployment is expected to be triggered by git push, records the commit/branch that should trigger the KVM pipeline, and records whether the deployment trigger was verified, unverified, skipped in dry-run mode, or failed. Fourteenth, update ARCHITECTURE_SPECS.md, .claude/README.md, .claude/pod-bridge.example.json, and the JSON schema file so future agents understand that ARCHITECTURE_SPECS.md is the shared spec file, that the filesystem is the durable message bus, that the Python bridge owns task movement, that claude -p with JSON output is the preferred headless execution path, that Greptile is the confidence gate, that Git push is the post-build deployment trigger, that the deployment trigger must be verified, and that infrastructure deployment is a downstream KVM stage controlled by repository automation and local configuration. Do not modify unrelated application source code.
acceptance_criteria: The task pod schema requires task_id, priority, spec_file, spec, acceptance_criteria, and files, with priority limited to high, med, or low.
ARCHITECTURE_SPECS.md is documented as the canonical shared spec file that both Manus as architecture agent and Claude Code as implementation agent must read before code changes.
The active task pod includes spec_file set to ARCHITECTURE_SPECS.md.
CLAUDE.md explicitly defines Claude Code as the Pod City Implementation Agent and states that it monitors ./pods/inbox/ for task JSON files.
CLAUDE.md instructs Claude Code to read both the active task JSON and the shared spec_file before modifying files, then validate requirements against the codebase.

CLAUDE.md includes CI Review Standards for Greptile or Greploop review context, including secure defaults, parameterized queries where database code is changed, least-privilege configuration, no hardcoded secrets, explicit tests, and no unrelated changes.
A Python bridge script exists at .claude/scripts/bridge.py or .claude/scripts/watch_pod_inbox.py and monitors ./pods/inbox/ for task.json and other *.json task pods.
The bridge supports watchdog-based monitoring and includes a polling fallback or clear dependency instructions if watchdog is missing.
The bridge waits for a detected task file to become stable before reading or moving it.
The bridge validates task JSON fields, including spec_file, before invoking Claude Code and moves invalid tasks to ./pods/failed/ with an explanatory result note.
The bridge moves tasks from ./pods/inbox/ to ./pods/active/ during execution, then to ./pods/archive/ on success or ./pods/failed/ on failure.
The Claude Code command is configurable and uses claude -p as the preferred non-interactive execution pattern when the claude command is available.

The default headless command template is equivalent to claude -p "Read ARCHITECTURE_SPECS.md and implement the task defined in <task-file>. Return machine-readable JSON describing success, changed files, tests, review requirements, infrastructure requirements, git handoff status, and notes." --allowedTools "Bash,Read,Edit" --max-turns 10 --output-format json.
The bridge does not use interactive watch mode as its default execution mechanism.
The bridge supports an alternate claude-code --execute --input <task-file> style command through configuration when available.

The bridge supports structured output when the installed Claude Code command provides JSON output, --output-format json, or --json-schema, and documents fallback behavior when structured output is unavailable.

The bridge parses structured JSON output to determine success status, changed files, tests, review requirements, infrastructure requirements, git handoff status, and notes before making lifecycle decisions.
If structured output is unavailable, the bridge captures stdout and stderr but only accepts conservative, explicitly configured success signals; it does not infer success from vague prose.
The bridge exposes configurable allowed tools and max-turns settings so headless runs are bounded and do not pause for unsupported tool permissions or enter endless loops.
The bridge verifies whether required execution environment variables such as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY are present before invoking Claude Code, without printing or storing secret values.
The bridge does not include --dangerously-skip-permissions in the committed default command or example that is enabled by default.
If --dangerously-skip-permissions is supported, it is documented only as a risky local opt-in in git-ignored configuration, disabled by default, and never required for normal operation.
The bridge captures stdout, stderr, exit code, timestamps, changed-file metadata where available, git handoff metadata, and lifecycle decisions in .claude/logs/ without committing local logs.
The bridge runs Greptile or Greploop as a separate post-execution review step rather than relying on the same generation context as the reviewer.
The bridge runs greptile review --path . when the Greptile CLI is available and requires confidence >= 5 before archiving or pushing a task.
The documentation explains how to enable the Greptile plugin in Claude Code using /plugins and how to run /greploop or /check-pr manually when needed.
If Greptile is unavailable or confidence is below 5, the task is annotated and moved to ./pods/failed/ unless an explicit documented local bypass flag is enabled.
The lifecycle directories ./pods/inbox/, ./pods/active/, ./pods/archive/, and ./pods/failed/ exist and contain .gitkeep placeholders where needed.

The bridge includes a post-quality Git handoff stage that can stage task-approved files, create an automation commit, and push to the configured remote branch to trigger repository deployment automation.
The Git handoff includes a dry-run mode that prints the exact git status, add, commit, and push commands without executing them.
A real git push is controlled by local configuration, verifies the target branch and remote, and refuses to commit secrets, .claude/logs/, .claude/pod-bridge.local.json, or unrelated changes.
The task is archived only after successful Claude execution, passing quality review, and successful required Git handoff, or after an explicitly configured dry-run/local-development bypass.

After a real git push, the bridge records the pushed branch and commit SHA, then verifies the KVM deployment trigger through configured GitHub Actions checks, deployment statuses, repository webhooks, a configured CI status command, or another explicit local verification command.
If no deployment automation is discoverable in the repository or local configuration, the bridge reports that the KVM trigger cannot be verified and does not claim production deployment success.
The task result metadata records deployment trigger status as verified, unverified, skipped_dry_run, or failed.
The infrastructure handoff is documented as a downstream repository-deployment stage triggered by Git push rather than a direct Manus provisioning action.
Infrastructure commands for KVM8, Terraform, or Ansible are disabled by default and require explicit local ignored configuration before any real provisioning command can run from the bridge.

By default, the infrastructure stage logs the expected deployment trigger, target branch, commit SHA when available, deployment-trigger verification status, and infrastructure requirements without executing destructive or provisioning actions.

ARCHITECTURE_SPECS.md, .claude/README.md, .claude/pod-bridge.example.json, and .claude/schemas/pod-task.schema.json describe the shared spec file, watcher lifecycle, schema, quality gate, headless claude -p JSON execution, permission-bypass policy, Git push deployment trigger, deployment-trigger verification, structured output expectations, failure handling, and durable filesystem message-bus pattern.
No unrelated application source code is modified as part of this bridge task.
